title: Switching Off an Essential Gene With Heat
endLine: Switch an essential protein off with heat; read when it acts.

scenes.tts: How do you study a gene a cell cannot live without? Break it permanently, and cells stop growing before you can test them. You need a switch you can flip on demand.
scenes.caption: How do you study a gene a cell cannot live without? Break it permanently, and cells stop growing before you can test them. You need a switch you can flip on demand.
scenes.visual: A dark microscope field filling 70% of frame height shows gently drifting budding yeast cells (schematic) beside a vertical temperature gauge on the right. Inside one yeast cell, a simple glowing gear icon (schematic, no molecular structure) is crossed out; the cells stall and fade away before a colony can form, leaving a bold bright question mark. The drifting yeast field smoothly returns as a glowing switch icon appears next to the gauge.
scenes.narration: How do you study a gene a cell cannot live without? Break it permanently, and cells stop growing before you can test them. You need a switch you can flip on demand.

scenes.visual: The drifting budding yeast field and temperature gauge dim slightly behind crisp high-contrast title text: Switching Off an Essential Gene With Heat. Slow ambient drift of the cells continues so the frame never freezes.

scenes.tts: A temperature-sensitive mutant builds that switch into one protein. At a low temperature, it works, so budding yeast divide normally. Each bud shows the stage: none in G one, small in S, large by mitosis. Warm cells to the restrictive temperature, and that protein fails. Cells then stall with one uniform bud shape.

scenes.visual: Same microscope dish and temperature gauge (schematic). At the cool blue low setting, a glowing intact protein block (schematic, no molecular structure) drives budding yeast across all three labeled stages: no bud (G1), small bud (S), and large bud (mitosis). The gauge rises to warm amber, labeled Restrictive; the protein block cracks open (schematic), and every cell advances until all stall with the same bud shape (schematic: which shape depends on the mutant; show large bud here).

scenes.tts: Never assume a gene acts where cells stop. Picture a car filling at one station each lap. Close that station beforehand, and it stalls later that lap. The station is the execution point, when the gene is last needed. Where cells collect is the termination point, or arrest point.

scenes.visual: The yeast dish morphs smoothly into a circular cell-cycle track (schematic) with the temperature gauge still on the right and G1, S, and mitosis bud silhouettes around the ring. A glowing car icon orbits past a fuel-station gate labeled Execution point. As the gauge climbs to warm amber, the station gate closes just ahead of the car; the car rolls well past the closed station and halts at a red zone labeled Arrest point.
scenes.narration: Never assume a gene acts where cells stop. Picture a car filling at one station each lap. Close that station beforehand, and it stalls later that lap. The station is the execution point, when the gene is last needed. Where cells collect is the termination point, or arrest point.

scenes.tts: Picture a growing culture spread around the cycle. We raise the heat right after one cell passes the execution point. Does it stop on this lap, or finish this division and stall next lap?
scenes.caption: Picture a growing culture spread around the cycle. We raise the heat right after one cell passes the execution point. Does it stop on this lap, or finish this division and stall next lap?
scenes.visual: Same circular cell-cycle track (schematic), now carrying moving yeast cells spread evenly around the ring. One bright highlighted cell sits just past the Execution point gate as the temperature gauge slides up to warm amber and the gate snaps shut. Two dashed schematic arrows branch from that cell—one halting on this lap, one completing the lap—beneath the on-screen question: Stop now, or finish this lap?
scenes.narration: Picture a growing culture spread around the cycle. We raise the heat right after one cell passes the execution point. Does it stop on this lap, or finish this division and stall next lap?

scenes.visual: The cycle track holds with the highlighted cell gently pulsing just past the closed Execution point gate and the question Stop now, or finish this lap? clearly visible. A smooth 4.5-second countdown bar (schematic) fills along the bottom edge so the frame stays alive.

scenes.tts: It finishes this lap, because it already passed the station. Only on the next lap does it stall. Follow single cells after the shift: those past the station finish, those before it stall. So the fraction that finish locates the execution point. Switch an essential protein off with heat, and how cells stall reveals when it acts.

scenes.visual: The highlighted cell glides to the end of the current lap, divides into two, and stalls at the Arrest point on the next lap. Across the ring (schematic), cells already past the Execution point glow teal as they finish this lap while cells behind it stall earlier; a glowing arc bracket marks the finishing fraction pointing directly back to the Execution point gate.

scenes.tts: Two traps can mislead. First, stalled cells show the arrest point, not when the gene acted. Track single cells or pulse heat to find timing. Second, a screen's count of genes is its yield, not every gene needed. A double mutant looks like whichever single mutant blocks earlier, so double mutants order steps.

scenes.visual: The cycle track and temperature gauge shift left as two clean schematic checks appear on the right. Top check: a red cluster at Arrest point gives way to brief warm pulses pulsing on the temperature gauge. Bottom check: a short row of found-gene bins (schematic) sits beside a faint longer row labelled 'Not found'; then two single-mutant cells, each blocked at a different step of a three-step arrow, merge into one 'Double mutant' cell that stalls at the earlier block, locking the arrows into order (schematic).

scenes.tts: With those guards, heat switches unlocked major pathways. In 1970, Leland Hartwell, Joseph Culotti and Brian Reid described temperature-sensitive mutants of budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. They called them C D C, for cell division cycle. At a higher temperature, each stopped with one uniform shape.

scenes.visual: Returning to the yeast dish and temperature gauge (schematic), tagged 1970 Hartwell, Culotti & Reid. Three rows of budding yeast labeled cdc divide freely at the cool blue setting; as the gauge rises to warm amber, each mutant row locks into a distinct uniform bud shape (no bud, small bud, large bud; schematic examples) along the cell cycle.

scenes.tts: In 1979, Novick and Schekman reported sec one, a yeast mutant growing at twenty-five degrees Celsius. At thirty-seven degrees Celsius, it keeps making secretory enzymes and cannot release them. In 1980, Novick, Field and Schekman sorted one hundred eighty-eight clones trapping the enzyme invertase into twenty-three complementation groups. Each is roughly one gene. Double mutants ordered those steps in 1981.
scenes.caption: In 1979, Novick and Schekman reported sec1, a yeast mutant growing at 25 °C. At 37 °C, it keeps making secretory enzymes and cannot release them. In 1980, Novick, Field and Schekman sorted 188 clones trapping the enzyme invertase into 23 complementation groups. Each is roughly one gene. Double mutants ordered those steps in 1981.
scenes.visual: Same yeast cell and temperature gauge, now showing exact marks 25 °C (blue) and 37 °C (amber), tagged 'Novick & Schekman 1979; Novick, Field & Schekman 1980'. At 25 °C, glowing vesicles ferry enzymes to the cell surface and release them (schematic). At 37 °C, vesicles pile up trapped inside sec1. The frame widens schematically to a density tube sorting 188 clones into 23 groups (label 'screen yield'), then links them into an ordered chain labeled 1981 double mutants.

scenes.tts: Heat switches work in animals too. In 1990, Volker Hartenstein and James Posakony warmed fly pupae carrying a temperature-sensitive version of Notch, a signaling protein. Pulses between zero and fourteen hours after pupae formed removed Notch for chosen windows. Extra bristle precursors formed in place of skin cells. So heat timing reveals when a protein acts.

scenes.visual: The temperature gauge stays anchored on the right as the microscope view transitions to a fly pupa silhouette (schematic) above a timeline marked 0 to 14 hours, tagged 1990 Hartenstein & Posakony. Brief warm amber pulses flash across the gauge and timeline; on a schematic patch of developing skin, extra bright bristle-precursor dots emerge in place of plain skin cells and grow into normal bristles.
